results.name: fourth_example_prefix_broadening
results.description: For 4-example sets whose first three examples are also shown as a 3-example set (31,3,1 -> 31,3,1,15), yes rate on the 4-example set minus the 3-example set over shared non-example targets; observed above null means the fourth example broadens generalization more (narrows less) than the model's position-decaying evidence predicts.
results.code:
# name: fourth_example_prefix_broadening
# description: For 4-example sets whose first three examples are also shown as a 3-example set (31,3,1 -> 31,3,1,15), yes rate on the 4-example set minus the 3-example set over shared non-example targets; observed above null means the fourth example broadens generalization more (narrows less) than the model's position-decaying evidence predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    pre = s.where(pd.Series(n == 4, index=df.index)).str.rsplit(",", n=1).str[0]
    k = pd.DataFrame({"s": s.to_numpy(), "t": t, "r": r, "n": n, "pre": pre.to_numpy(), "isin": isin})
    k = k[~k["isin"]]
    three = k[k["n"] == 3].groupby(["s", "t"])["r"].mean().rename("r3").reset_index().rename(columns={"s": "pre"})
    four = k[k["n"] == 4].groupby(["pre", "t"])["r"].mean().rename("r4").reset_index()
    mm = four.merge(three, on=["pre", "t"])
    v = float((mm["r4"] - mm["r3"]).mean()) if len(mm) else 0.0
    return v if np.isfinite(v) else 0.0

results.name: near_extrapolation_large_minus_small_edge
results.description: For targets outside the examples' span at distance 1-10 from the nearest example, yes rate when that nearest example is >=50 minus when it is <=25; observed above null means people generalize further around large numbers (Weber-like relative width) than the model's equal-range prior predicts.
results.code:
# name: near_extrapolation_large_minus_small_edge
# description: For targets outside the examples' span at distance 1-10 from the nearest example, yes rate when that nearest example is >=50 minus when it is <=25; observed above null means people generalize further around large numbers (Weber-like relative width) than the model's equal-range prior predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    out = (t < mn) | (t > mx)
    near = np.where(t < mn, mn, mx)
    base = out & (nd >= 1) & (nd <= 10)
    return m(base & (near >= 50)) - m(base & (near <= 25))

results.name: single_example_above_minus_below
results.description: For one-example sets with the example in 15-85, yes rate on targets 1-10 above the example minus targets 1-10 below it; observed above null means people extend upward more than the model's symmetric equal-range prior predicts.
results.code:
# name: single_example_above_minus_below
# description: For one-example sets with the example in 15-85, yes rate on targets 1-10 above the example minus targets 1-10 below it; observed above null means people extend upward more than the model's symmetric equal-range prior predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    d = t - first
    base = (n == 1) & (first >= 15) & (first <= 85)

results.name: interior_yes_4ex_minus_2ex_matched_span
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets inside the span for 4-example sets minus 2-example sets, both restricted to spans of 20-60; observed above null means extra examples tighten in-span generalization less (or raise it more) than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: interior_yes_4ex_minus_2ex_matched_span
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets inside the span for 4-example sets minus 2-example sets, both restricted to spans of 20-60; observed above null means extra examples tighten in-span generalization less (or raise it more) than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    span = mx - mn
    base = ~isin & (t > mn) & (t < mx) & (span >= 20) & (span <= 60)
    return m(base & (n == 4)) - m(base & (n == 2))

results.name: single_example_multiple_target_yes
results.description: For one-example sets with example 3-25, yes rate on targets that are multiples of the example (excluding the example) minus yes rate on non-multiple targets more than 10 away; observed above null means people generalize to multiples of a lone example more than the model's rule prior predicts.
results.code:
# name: single_example_multiple_target_yes
# description: For one-example sets with example 3-25, yes rate on targets that are multiples of the example (excluding the example) minus yes rate on non-multiple targets more than 10 away; observed above null means people generalize to multiples of a lone example more than the model's rule prior predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.nan_to_num(first, nan=1).astype(int)
    e = np.maximum(e, 1)
    base = (n == 1) & (first >= 3) & (first <= 25) & ~isin
    mult = (t % e == 0)
    return m(base & mult) - m(base & ~mult & (nd > 10))

results.name: rule_violating_interior_yes
results.description: For sets of 3-4 examples that all share a last digit or are all multiples of some k in 3-12, the yes rate on non-example targets inside the examples' span that break every such shared rule; observed below null means people reject in-span rule violators more strongly than the model (its range hypotheses over-generalize when a rule fits).
results.code:
# name: rule_violating_interior_yes
# description: For sets of 3-4 examples that all share a last digit or are all multiples of some k in 3-12, the yes rate on non-example targets inside the examples' span that break every such shared rule; observed below null means people reject in-span rule violators more strongly than the model (its range hypotheses over-generalize when a rule fits).
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    for c in range(x.shape[1], 4):
        x[c] = np.nan
    x = x.iloc[:, :4]
    X = x.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.isfinite(X).sum(axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    isin = (X == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    nd = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    def m(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    Xi = np.nan_to_num(X, nan=-1).astype(int)
    valid = np.isfinite(X)
    ok = np.zeros(len(X), bool)
    viol = np.ones(len(X), bool)
    ld = Xi % 10
    same_ld = np.all((ld == ld[:, :1]) | ~valid, axis=1)
    ok |= same_ld
    viol &= ~(same_ld & (t % 10 == ld[:, 0]))
    for k in range(3, 13):
        allk = np.all((Xi % k == 0) | ~valid, axis=1)
        ok |= allk
        viol &= ~(allk & (t % k == 0))
    mask = (n >= 3) & ok & viol & ~isin & (t > mn) & (t < mx)
    return m(mask)

results.name: two_example_interior_wide_minus_narrow_gap
results.description: For two-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets strictly between the examples when the gap is >=40 minus when the gap is <=20; observed above null means people fill wide gaps more than the model's size-principle ranges predict (observed below null: less).
